The published course material begins with the architectural background and then follows the modern language-model lifecycle from data to release.

## Published material

**Introduction.** Recurrent neural networks, LSTMs, attention, the original Transformer, and the encoder-only, decoder-only, and encoder–decoder families.

**Lecture 1: The frontier language-model lifecycle.** The historical transitions that changed model interfaces, training, evaluation, inference-time computation, multimodality, and the economics of AI infrastructure.

**Lecture 2: Data, training signals, and capability boundaries.** Observed, human-labeled, self-supervised, synthetic, and evaluation data; collection and annotation systems; pretraining and post-training signals; benchmark interpretation; distillation; and measured cases where specialized models outperform LLM-based systems.

**Lecture 3: Corpus design, acquisition, and provenance.** Target populations and acquisition frames; reproducible snapshots; multilingual and teacher-generated source portfolios; acquisition yield and coverage audits; record identity, rights, and provenance.

**Lecture 4: Document extraction, quality filtering, and corpus auditing.** Recovering text and structure from acquired objects; explicit extraction references; normalization and language identification; quality decisions; retained and rejected audits; and pipeline order, cost, and evidence.

**Lecture 5: Corpus integrity—deduplication, contamination, and privacy.** Exact and canonical equality; shingling, Jaccard, MinHash/LSH, clustering, and representative selection; family-aware benchmark decontamination; sensitive-span handling; integrity audits; and reproducible corpus locks.

**Lecture 6: Tokenization and sequence construction.** Byte-level BPE and unigram segmentation; vocabulary and representation trade-offs; multilingual tokenizer audits; special tokens and chat formats; multimodal embeddings; next-token targets; document boundaries; attention and loss masks; long-document handling; and packing.

**Lecture 7: Data mixtures, multilingual exposure, and scaling.** Record probabilities versus realized loss-bearing targets; finite-source coverage and repetition; multilingual, domain, and origin allocation; continued pretraining and replay; controlled mixture experiments; compute-optimal and data-constrained scaling; DoReMi, RegMix, and staged curricula.

**Lecture 8: Evaluation from perplexity to real tasks.** Versioned evaluation protocols; likelihood, perplexity, and bits per byte; task checks, calibration, abstention, pass at k, majority voting, inference costs, paired comparisons, and family-level uncertainty.

**Lecture 9: Continued pretraining, SFT, and instruction data.** Domain adaptation and replay; instruction demonstrations and response-only loss; chat templates and tool-result masking; LoRA and measured adaptation–retention trade-offs.
